claims.statement: The 2005 ISHLT scheme defines cardiac acute cellular rejection as 0R, 1R, 2R, and 3R using infiltrate and myocyte-damage criteria.
Full pathological AMR categorization combines histological and immunopathological findings, so H&E-only morphology is not equivalent to complete pAMR classification.
Multicenter studies show that WSI models can detect cardiac allograft rejection, but each study's validation scope must remain explicit.
Internal cross-validation can overstate transportability: cardiac rejection performance varied materially across independent cohorts.
Handcrafted morphologic features are a credible ACR grading comparator, but that evidence does not extend to AMR or future rejection prediction.
GSE290577 is a longitudinal spatial-transcriptomic tissue-core resource, not an independent routine-WSI screening cohort.
CLAM supports slide-label-only WSI classification and attention heatmaps, but its original evidence is not cardiac-specific and does not make attention causal explanation.
UNI is a large-scale pathology patch encoder whose local cardiac and stain-specific value still requires task-specific aggregation and ablation.
Attention-based MIL provides learnable permutation-invariant bag pooling and instance weights, not automatically validated causal explanations.
TransMIL is a reasonable contextual-MIL comparator because it models inter-instance correlations, but superiority is task dependent.
Cross-laboratory stain variation can harm transfer, so stain augmentation and normalization should be evaluated as robustness interventions rather than assumptions.
TRIPOD+AI is the reporting framework for transparent clinical prediction-model studies, including clustered performance, calibration, uncertainty, fairness, and open science.
PROBAST+AI appraises development quality and evaluation risk of bias and applicability across participants/data, predictors, outcomes, and analysis.
Repeated biopsies and center clusters must be made explicit in the evaluation and reporting plan to avoid ambiguous independence and leakage claims.
A distinct MIL aggregation comparator.
A concrete hierarchical representation comparator.
A bag-learning strategy to test under identical splits.
Acquisition source can carry target-correlated shortcuts.
An encoder comparator beyond UNI.
Calibration needs its own assessment.
Stains can supply representation-learning supervision.
A concrete multistain fusion design without pixel correspondence.
Histologic grade and clinical severity are distinct prediction targets.
Spatial multiscale feature fusion differs from probability late fusion.
Laboratory ordering and timing carry survival-related information even without using test values.
GRU-D incorporates observation masks and time intervals to exploit informative missingness in time-series prediction.
Precision-recall complements ROC by examining true positives among positive predictions in imbalanced classification.

In the examined logistic-regression settings, undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE did not improve discrimination and overestimated minority-class probabilities; sensitivity and specificity could also be changed by adjusting the decision threshold.

In the examined machine-learning prediction settings, class imbalance corrections often overestimated risk; uncorrected models had similar or better calibration, and recalibration did not invariably remove the problem.
MCC incorporates all four confusion-matrix categories; the examined examples show how accuracy and F1 alone can give misleading impressions under imbalance.
For well-calibrated conditional probabilities, the F1-optimal threshold is half the optimal F1; for an uninformative classifier, maximizing F1 can label every example positive.
Variance in a finite-sample model-selection criterion can lead to overfitting of that criterion and selection bias in subsequent performance evaluation.
Small-sample cross-validation can have substantial uncertainty, and standard errors calculated across folds can underestimate that uncertainty.
Required sample size depends on participants, outcome frequency, anticipated predictive performance and candidate parameters; a fixed events-per-variable rule is not a universal adequacy criterion.
Biopsy-sized samples from autopsied cardiac allografts were compared with larger sections of the same hearts; the authors concluded that routine biopsies may underestimate middle grades of rejection.

The study re-examined available post-transplant endomyocardial biopsies and transplanted-heart autopsy tissue, with two cardiac pathologists blinded to prior reports, to relate pathology including acute myocardial injury to clinical outcomes.

Two tuberculosis autopsy cases supplied annotated positive acid-fast bacilli, and forty AFB-negative biopsy cases supplied background/artifact examples for CNN training, followed by application to bronchoscopy specimens.
A model pretrained on GTEx tissue-type recognition was transferred to renal glomerulus, arteriole and artery segmentation; the paper identifies GTEx WSIs as autopsy tissue.

Heart-transplant autopsies included both graft-related and non-graft-related deaths; infection was the most frequent cause of death. The abstract also reports moderate/severe ACR in a patient with a recently negative biopsy.
In the renal vessel-segmentation comparison, GTEx pretraining outperformed random initialization but ImageNet pretraining achieved higher MCC than GTEx for glomeruli, arterioles and arteries.
Autopsy-acquired cardiac allografts were used to examine biopsy grading reliability as a function of the morphological diagnostic criterion and the number of fragments.

In hearts known to have lymphocytic myocarditis at autopsy, biopsy-sized specimens frequently missed diagnostic inflammation, illustrating spatial sampling error even when multiple specimens were examined.
Biopsy C4d immunoreactivity was associated with subsequent cardiac allograft vasculopathy and death; autopsy findings were used in the outcome assessment of a deceased subset.

The study compared earlier right-ventricular biopsy fibrosis with later whole-heart fibrosis in the same patients, combining 52 explant and 18 autopsy cases; biopsy-to-excision time was explicitly considered.
SongCi learned representations from postmortem WSI and text; the main article also reports transfer evaluation on three clinical WSI datasets and five patch datasets, beyond forensic tasks.
Despite biopsy-oriented framing, the reported experiment used 60 microscopic images from six autopsy subjects; it did not test transfer to living-patient endomyocardial biopsies.

The study excluded currently high-grade ACR, pAMR >=1 and treated rejection from study biopsies, then analyzed stromal morphology over time against prior inflammatory histories and subsequent allograft-loss/CAV outcomes.
The authors report limited routine AMR immunostaining and historical diagnostic-label variability; the cohort is single-center and the analysis links repeated biopsies to patient-level outcomes.
CONCH pretraining aligns histopathology images and captions; downstream supervised WSI classification uses pretrained tile features with ABMIL, whereas ROI classification uses logistic regression.
The CONCH preprint omits CTransPath from TCGA slide-level comparisons due to possible pretraining/test overlap, and its zero-shot WSI method reports the best pooling K among several choices.

TITAN pretraining includes GTEx alongside clinical pathology and multiple stains, uses CONCHv1.5 patch features, and evaluates fixed slide embeddings with logistic regression and few-shot class prototypes against mean-pooling and ABMIL baselines.

TITAN includes renal allograft rejection (4847 H&E WSIs from 1118 patients). Its renal dataset paragraph describes label-stratified slide counts, while its survival protocol selects a penalty using the best average test metric across folds.
